claim: The use of siblings to infer the factors influencing complex traits has been a cornerstone of quantitative genetics.
source: The use of siblings to infer the factors influencing complex traits has been a cornerstone of quantitative genetics.
evidence: This is a general statement about the historical use of siblings in quantitative genetics, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Individuals with extreme trait values (e.g. in the top 1%) are at the greatest risk of disease.
source: Inferring the genetic architecture most relevant to this group of individuals is important because they are at the greatest risk of disease and may be more likely to harbour rare variants of large effect due to natural selection.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relationship between extreme trait values and disease risk.

claim: Individuals with extreme trait values may be more likely to harbour rare variants of large effect due to natural selection.
source: Inferring the genetic architecture most relevant to this group of individuals is important because they are at the greatest risk of disease and may be more likely to harbour rare variants of large effect due to natural selection.
evidence: This is based on inference about the relationship between natural selection and rare variants in extreme trait values.

claim: The theoretical framework derives expected distributions of sibling trait values based on an index sibling's trait value, estimated trait heritability, and null assumptions.
source: We develop a theoretical framework that derives expected distributions of sibling trait values based on an index sibling's trait value, estimated trait heritability, and null assumptions that include infinitesimal genetic effects and environmental factors that are either controlled for or have combined Gaussian effects.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the manuscript.

claim: The null assumptions include infinitesimal genetic effects and environmental factors that are either controlled for or have combined Gaussian effects.
source: We develop a theoretical framework that derives expected distributions of sibling trait values based on an index sibling's trait value, estimated trait heritability, and null assumptions that include infinitesimal genetic effects and environmental factors that are either controlled for or have combined Gaussian effects.
evidence: This describes the specific assumptions used in the theoretical framework.

claim: The statistical tests can distinguish between trait tails characterised by common polygenic architecture from those that include substantial enrichments of de novo or rare variant (Mendelian) architecture.
source: This framework is then used to develop statistical tests powered to distinguish between trait tails characterised by common polygenic architecture from those that include substantial enrichments of de novo or rare variant (Mendelian) architecture.
evidence: This describes the capability of the statistical tests developed in the study.

claim: The tests can be used to infer genetic architecture in any cohort or health registry that includes siblings and their trait values.
source: We apply our tests to UK Biobank data here, although we note that they can be used to infer genetic architecture in any cohort or health registry that includes siblings and their trait values, since these tests do not use genetic data.
evidence: This describes the broad applicability of the tests.

claim: The tests do not use genetic data.
source: We apply our tests to UK Biobank data here, although we note that they can be used to infer genetic architecture in any cohort or health registry that includes siblings and their trait values, since these tests do not use genetic data.
evidence: This is a key feature of the methodology described.

claim: Fisher (1919) developed theory for estimating heritability using siblings.
source: The fields of quantitative genetics and genetic epidemiology have exploited the shared genetics and environment of siblings in many applications, notably to estimate heritability, using theory developed a century ago (Fisher, 1919; Lush, 1940), and more recently to infer a so-called 'household effect' (Selzam et al., 2018), which contributes to genetic risk indirectly via correlation between genetics and household environment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher's work.

claim: Lush (1940) developed theory for estimating heritability using siblings.
source: The fields of quantitative genetics and genetic epidemiology have exploited the shared genetics and environment of siblings in many applications, notably to estimate heritability, using theory developed a century ago (Fisher, 1919; Lush, 1940), and more recently to infer a so-called 'household effect' (Selzam et al., 2018), which contributes to genetic risk indirectly via correlation between genetics and household environment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lush's work.

claim: A 'household effect' contributes to genetic risk indirectly via correlation between genetics and household environment.
source: The fields of quantitative genetics and genetic epidemiology have exploited the shared genetics and environment of siblings in many applications, notably to estimate heritability, using theory developed a century ago (Fisher, 1919; Lush, 1940), and more recently to infer a so-called 'household effect' (Selzam et al., 2018), which contributes to genetic risk indirectly via correlation between genetics and household environment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Selzam et al., 2018.

claim: The genetic architecture of a complex trait is typically inferred from findings of multiple independent studies including GWAS, sequencing studies, and family sequencing studies.
source: The genetic architecture of a complex trait is typically inferred from findings of multiple independent studies: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identifying common variants (Yengo et al., 2022; Selvaraj et al., 2022), whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing studies detecting rare variants (Singh et al., 2022), and family sequencing studies designed to identify de novo and rare Mendelian mutations (Iyegbe and O'Reilly, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing different study types.

claim: GWAS identify common variants.
source: The genetic architecture of a complex trait is typically inferred from findings of multiple independent studies: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identifying common variants (Yengo et al., 2022; Selvaraj et al., 2022), whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing studies detecting rare variants (Singh et al., 2022), and family sequencing studies designed to identify de novo and rare Mendelian mutations (Iyegbe and O'Reilly, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yengo et al., 2022 and Selvaraj et al., 2022.

claim: Whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing studies detect rare variants.
source: The genetic architecture of a complex trait is typically inferred from findings of multiple independent studies: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identifying common variants (Yengo et al., 2022; Selvaraj et al., 2022), whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing studies detecting rare variants (Singh et al., 2022), and family sequencing studies designed to identify de novo and rare Mendelian mutations (Iyegbe and O'Reilly, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2022.

claim: Family sequencing studies are designed to identify de novo and rare Mendelian mutations.
source: The genetic architecture of a complex trait is typically inferred from findings of multiple independent studies: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identifying common variants (Yengo et al., 2022; Selvaraj et al., 2022), whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing studies detecting rare variants (Singh et al., 2022), and family sequencing studies designed to identify de novo and rare Mendelian mutations (Iyegbe and O'Reilly, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iyegbe and O'Reilly, 2022.

claim: The relative contribution of each type of variant to trait heritability is a function of historical selection pressures on the trait in the population.
source: The relative contribution of each type of variant to trait heritability is a function of historical selection pressures on the trait in the population (Koch et al., 2024; Uricchio, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koch et al., 2024 and Uricchio, 2020.

claim: If selection has recently acted to increase the average value of a trait, then the lower tail of the trait distribution may become enriched for large-effect rare variants over time.
source: If selection has recently acted to increase the average value of a trait, then the lower tail of the trait distribution may become enriched for large-effect rare variants over time because trait-reducing alleles will be subject to negative selection, and so those with large effects – most likely to 'push' individuals to the lower tail – will be reduced to low frequencies (Corte et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corte et al., 2023 and represents inference about evolutionary processes.

claim: Trait-reducing alleles will be subject to negative selection when selection acts to increase the average value of a trait.
source: If selection has recently acted to increase the average value of a trait, then the lower tail of the trait distribution may become enriched for large-effect rare variants over time because trait-reducing alleles will be subject to negative selection, and so those with large effects – most likely to 'push' individuals to the lower tail – will be reduced to low frequencies (Corte et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary theory and supported by citation.

claim: If the trait is subject to stabilising selection, then both tails of the trait distribution may be enriched for rare variant aetiology.
source: Similarly, if the trait is subject to stabilising selection, then both tails of the trait distribution may be enriched for rare variant aetiology (Momozawa and Mizukami, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Momozawa and Mizukami, 2021.

claim: Enrichment of rare variants in trait tails can result in less accurate polygenic scores in the tails of the trait distribution.
source: This can result in less accurate polygenic scores in the tails of the trait distribution (Chan et al., 2011) and can also produce dissimilarity between siblings beyond what is expected under polygenicity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2011.

claim: Enrichment of rare variants in trait tails can produce dissimilarity between siblings beyond what is expected under polygenicity.
source: This can result in less accurate polygenic scores in the tails of the trait distribution (Chan et al., 2011) and can also produce dissimilarity between siblings beyond what is expected under polygenicity.
evidence: This is based on inference about the effects of rare variants on sibling similarity.

claim: Studies on the intellectual ability of sibling pairs have demonstrated similarity for average intellectual ability.
source: For example, studies on the intellectual ability of sibling pairs have demonstrated similarity for average intellectual ability (Shakeshaft et al., 2015), regression-to-the-mean for siblings at the upper tail of the distribution (Shakeshaft et al., 2015), and complete discordance when one sibling is at the lower extreme tail of the distribution (Reichenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shakeshaft et al., 2015.

claim: Studies on the intellectual ability of sibling pairs have demonstrated regression-to-the-mean for siblings at the upper tail of the distribution.
source: For example, studies on the intellectual ability of sibling pairs have demonstrated similarity for average intellectual ability (Shakeshaft et al., 2015), regression-to-the-mean for siblings at the upper tail of the distribution (Shakeshaft et al., 2015), and complete discordance when one sibling is at the lower extreme tail of the distribution (Reichenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shakeshaft et al., 2015.

claim: Studies on the intellectual ability of sibling pairs have demonstrated complete discordance when one sibling is at the lower extreme tail of the distribution.
source: For example, studies on the intellectual ability of sibling pairs have demonstrated similarity for average intellectual ability (Shakeshaft et al., 2015), regression-to-the-mean for siblings at the upper tail of the distribution (Shakeshaft et al., 2015), and complete discordance when one sibling is at the lower extreme tail of the distribution (Reichenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reichenberg et al., 2016.

claim: No theoretical framework has been developed to formally infer genetic architecture from sibling trait data.
source: However, no theoretical framework has been developed to formally infer genetic architecture from sibling trait data.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that this work addresses.

claim: When an individual's extreme trait value (top 1%) is due to many alleles of small effect ('polygenic'), then their siblings' trait values are expected to show regression-to-the-mean.
source: Left to right: When an individual's extreme trait value (top 1%) is due to many alleles of small effect ('polygenic'), then their siblings' trait values are expected to show regression-to-the-mean (grey).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents a theoretical prediction based on polygenic architecture.

claim: When an individual's extreme trait value is due to a de novo mutation of large effect, then their siblings are expected to have trait values that correspond to the background distribution.
source: When an individual's extreme trait value is due to a de novo mutation of large effect, then their siblings are expected to have trait values that correspond to the background distribution (green).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents a theoretical prediction based on de novo mutations.

claim: When an individual's extreme trait value is the result of an inherited rare allele of large effect ('Mendelian'), then their siblings are expected to have either similarly extreme trait values or trait values that are drawn from the background distribution, depending on whether or not they inherited the same large effect allele.
source: When an individual's extreme trait value is the result of an inherited rare allele of large effect ('Mendelian'), then their siblings are expected to have either similarly extreme trait values or trait values that are drawn from the background distribution (red), depending on whether or not they inherited the same large effect allele.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and represents a theoretical prediction based on Mendelian inheritance.

claim: Assuming completely polygenic (i.e. infinitesimal) architecture, siblings of individuals with extreme trait values are expected to be less extreme.
source: Assuming completely polygenic (i.e. infinitesimal) architecture, siblings of individuals with extreme trait values are expected to be less extreme.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on polygenic architecture.

claim: Regression-to-the-mean can be understood through two factors: (i) average genetic contribution of the parents (mid-parent) to the trait value and (ii) random genetic reassortment occurring during meiosis.
source: This regression-to-the-mean can be understood through the two factors (Falconer and Mackay, 1983; Alberts et al., 2002) that determine inherited genetic variation: (i) average genetic contribution of the parents (mid-parent) to the trait value and (ii) random genetic reassortment occurring during meiosis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Falconer and Mackay, 1983 and Alberts et al., 2002.

claim: Excess discordance between siblings is indicative of an enrichment of de novo mutations.
source: These tests leverage the fact that the similarity (or dissimilarity) in trait values among siblings provides information about the underlying genetic architecture (see Figure 1). For example, high-impact de novo mutations generate large dissimilarity between siblings when only one carries the unique mutant allele, while Mendelian variants can create excess similarity in the tails of the distribution when siblings both inherit the same mutant allele.
evidence: This is based on inference about the effects of de novo mutations on sibling similarity.

claim: Excess concordance between siblings indicates an enrichment of Mendelian variants.
source: These tests leverage the fact that the similarity (or dissimilarity) in trait values among siblings provides information about the underlying genetic architecture (see Figure 1). For example, high-impact de novo mutations generate large dissimilarity between siblings when only one carries the unique mutant allele, while Mendelian variants can create excess similarity in the tails of the distribution when siblings both inherit the same mutant allele.
evidence: This is based on inference about the effects of Mendelian variants on sibling similarity.

claim: Power to identify de novo architecture is greatest when heritability is high.
source: These tests demonstrate that power to identify de novo architecture is greatest when heritability is high, while power to identify Mendelian architecture is greatest when heritability is low.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Power to identify Mendelian architecture is greatest when heritability is low.
source: These tests demonstrate that power to identify de novo architecture is greatest when heritability is high, while power to identify Mendelian architecture is greatest when heritability is low.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: When heritability is estimated near 50% and at least 0.1% of the population has high-impact rare aetiology, both tests are well-powered to identify each class of complex tail architecture.
source: When heritability is estimated near 50% and at least 0.1% of the population has high-impact rare aetiology, both tests are well-powered to identify each class of complex tail architecture.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The UK Biobank includes data from over 21,000 siblings.
source: The UK Biobank includes data from over 21,000 siblings (Lello et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lello et al., 2023.

claim: Expected polygenic architecture was observed in both tails for Ankle Spacing.
source: We observed expected polygenic architecture in both tails for Ankle Spacing.
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mendelian architecture was inferred in the lower tail for Urate.
source: We inferred Mendelian architecture in the lower tail for Urate and the upper tail for Wait Circumference and Left Hand Grip Strength.
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mendelian architecture was inferred in the upper tail for Waist Circumference.
source: We inferred Mendelian architecture in the lower tail for Urate and the upper tail for Wait Circumference and Left Hand Grip Strength.
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mendelian architecture was inferred in the upper tail for Left Hand Grip Strength.
source: We inferred Mendelian architecture in the lower tail for Urate and the upper tail for Wait Circumference and Left Hand Grip Strength.
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: De novo architecture was inferred in the lower tail for Forced Expiratory Volume.
source: De novo architecture was inferred in the lower tail for Forced Expiratory Volume and strongly inferred in both tails for Sitting Height, which is supported by evidence from deep sequencing studies indicating that rare variants play a substantial role in the genetic aetiology for this trait (Tcheandjieu et al., 2020; Bjornsdottir et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: De novo architecture was strongly inferred in both tails for Sitting Height.
source: De novo architecture was inferred in the lower tail for Forced Expiratory Volume and strongly inferred in both tails for Sitting Height, which is supported by evidence from deep sequencing studies indicating that rare variants play a substantial role in the genetic aetiology for this trait (Tcheandjieu et al., 2020; Bjornsdottir et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Deep sequencing studies indicate that rare variants play a substantial role in the genetic aetiology for Sitting Height.
source: De novo architecture was inferred in the lower tail for Forced Expiratory Volume and strongly inferred in both tails for Sitting Height, which is supported by evidence from deep sequencing studies indicating that rare variants play a substantial role in the genetic aetiology for this trait (Tcheandjieu et al., 2020; Bjornsdottir et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tcheandjieu et al., 2020 and Bjornsdottir et al., 2022.

claim: In the lower tail for Left Hand Grip Strength, both de novo and Mendelian architecture were inferred.
source: In the lower tail for Left Hand Grip Strength, we infer the presence of both de novo (greater than expected mean) and Mendelian (more concordant siblings than expected) architecture.
evidence: This is a result from applying the tests to UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The theoretical framework could be extended to applications such as estimating heritability, characterising mating patterns, and inferring historical selection pressures.
source: Our novel framework can be extended to applications such as estimating heritability, characterising mating patterns, and inferring historical selection pressures.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the framework.

claim: Departures from the expected conditional sibling trait distributions could be due to environmental risk factors rather than rare genetic architecture.
source: First and foremost, departures from the expected conditional sibling trait distributions could be due to environmental risk factors, such as medication-use or work-related exposures, rather than rare genetic architecture.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Rejection of the null hypothesis from the tests should be considered only as indicating effects consistent with non-polygenic genetic architecture, alongside alternative explanations such as tail-specific unshared or shared environmental risks.
source: Rejection of the null hypothesis from our tests should be considered only as indicating effects consistent with non-polygenic genetic architecture, alongside alternative explanations such as tail-specific unshared (de novo) or shared ('Mendelian') environmental risks.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpretation of results.

claim: If shared environmental risk factors contribute significantly to trait similarity among siblings, then heritability estimates will be upwardly biased.
source: Secondly, our modelling assumes that the environmental risk factors of siblings are independent of each other. If in fact shared environmental risk factors contribute significantly to trait similarity among siblings, then our heritability estimates will be upwardly biased.
evidence: This is based on inference about the effects of shared environment on heritability estimates.

claim: A large meta-analysis of heritability estimates from twin studies concluded that the contribution of shared environment among siblings is insubstantial.
source: Moreover, a large meta-analysis of heritability estimates from twin studies (Polderman et al., 2015) concluded that the contribution of shared environment among siblings (even twins) is insubstantial, and so we might expect this to have a limited impact on results from our tests.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Polderman et al., 2015.

claim: The modelling assumes random mating.
source: Thirdly, our modelling assumes random mating, and so the results from our tests in relation to traits that may be the subject of assortative mating should be considered with caution.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: The modelling assumes additivity of genetic effects.
source: Likewise, our modelling assumes additivity of genetic effects, and so, while additivity is well-supported by much statistical genetics research (Wray et al., 2018; Hivert et al., 2021), results from our tests should be reconsidered for any traits with evidence for significant non-additive genetic effects.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model, supported by citations to Wray et al., 2018 and Hivert et al., 2021.

claim: Additivity of genetic effects is well-supported by much statistical genetics research.
source: Likewise, our modelling assumes additivity of genetic effects, and so, while additivity is well-supported by much statistical genetics research (Wray et al., 2018; Hivert et al., 2021), results from our tests should be reconsidered for any traits with evidence for significant non-additive genetic effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wray et al., 2018 and Hivert et al., 2021.

claim: The approach provides a novel way of inferring genetic architecture without genetic data.
source: Our approach not only provides a novel way of inferring genetic architecture (without genetic data) but can do so specifically in the tails of trait distributions, which are most likely to harbour complex genetic architecture, due to selection, and are a key focus in biomedical research given their enrichment for disease.
evidence: This is a summary of the key contribution of the work.

claim: Trait tails are most likely to harbour complex genetic architecture due to selection.
source: Our approach not only provides a novel way of inferring genetic architecture (without genetic data) but can do so specifically in the tails of trait distributions, which are most likely to harbour complex genetic architecture, due to selection, and are a key focus in biomedical research given their enrichment for disease.
evidence: This is based on inference about the effects of selection on trait distributions.

claim: Trait tails are a key focus in biomedical research given their enrichment for disease.
source: Our approach not only provides a novel way of inferring genetic architecture (without genetic data) but can do so specifically in the tails of trait distributions, which are most likely to harbour complex genetic architecture, due to selection, and are a key focus in biomedical research given their enrichment for disease.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relationship between extreme trait values and disease.

claim: The conditional sibling trait distribution provides a simple way of understanding the expected trait values of individuals according to their sibling's trait value.
source: The conditional sibling trait distribution provides a simple way of understanding the expected trait values of individuals according to their sibling's trait value, which could be used to answer questions of societal importance and inform future research.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the derived distribution.

claim: Further development of the theory could lead to applications such as estimating levels of assortative mating, inferring historical selection pressures, and quantifying heritability in specific strata of the population.
source: Moreover, further development of the theory described here could lead to a range of other applications, for example, estimating levels of assortative mating, inferring historical selection pressures, and quantifying heritability in specific strata of the population.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the framework.

claim: The tests are well calibrated as demonstrated by null simulations.
source: Null simulations (red dashed line) demonstrate tests are well calibrated.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Individuals inferred as having rare variants of large effect could undergo clinical genetic testing to identify potential pathogenic variants.
source: Firstly, those individuals inferred as having rare variants of large effect could be followed up in multiple ways to gain individual-level insights. For example, they could undergo clinical genetic testing to identify potential pathogenic variants with effects beyond the examined trait, either in the form of diseases or disorders that the individual has already been diagnosed with or else that they have yet to present with but may be at high future risk for.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The framework could help refine the design of sequencing studies for identifying rare variants of large effect.
source: Our framework could also help refine the design of sequencing studies for identifying rare variants of large effect.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the framework.

claim: The approach enables the identification of individuals that may be most likely to harbour rare variants, who could be prioritised for deep sequencing.
source: Since our approach enables the identification of individuals that may be most likely to harbour rare variants, then these individuals could be prioritised for (deep) sequencing.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the approach.

claim: The ability to distinguish between de novo and Mendelian architecture could influence study design, with de novo architecture suggesting that a family trio design may be more effective than population sequencing.
source: Moreover, our ability to distinguish between de novo and Mendelian architecture could influence the broad study design, with the former suggesting that a family trio design may be more effective than population sequencing, which may be favoured if Mendelian architecture is inferred.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The approach could be applied as a screening step to prioritise those traits, and corresponding tails, most likely to harbour rare variant architecture.
source: Furthermore, our approach could be applied as a screening step to prioritise those traits, and corresponding tails, most likely to harbour rare variant architecture.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the approach.

claim: If sequence data have already been collected, the approach could be utilised to increase the power of statistical methods for detecting rare variants by upweighting individuals most likely to harbour rare variants.
source: Finally, if sequence data have already been collected, either cohort-wide or using a more targeted design, then our approach could be utilised to increase the power of statistical methods for detecting rare variants by upweighting individuals most likely to harbour rare variants.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the approach.

claim: The theoretically derived conditional sibling trait distributions do not differ significantly from those generated from simulated data.
source: We compared the theoretical conditional sibling trait distributions to those generated from simulated data (see Appendix 3) and found that irrespective of the trait used to simulate data (e.g. fluid intelligence, height) the two distributions did not differ significantly, suggesting that our analytically derived distributions are a valid model for the conditional sibling trait distribution (Equation 4).
evidence: This is a validation result from comparing theoretical and simulated distributions.

claim: The statistical tests are robust to shared environmental effects with consistent effects throughout the trait distribution.
source: Polderman et al., 2015 found limited contribution of shared environment for most complex traits and, critically, our statistical tests are robust to shared environmental effects with consistent effects throughout the trait distribution (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is a claim about the robustness of the tests, supported by citation to Polderman et al., 2015.
